<div class="markdown"><p>Chapter 1 compressed an ordered sequence of coin flips into <code>(flips, heads)</code>. The compression worked for inferring which coin produced the data, but the chapter did not explain where that representation came from.</p><p>This chapter constructs the representation by composing transformations of the original representation. We will specify a small operation that changes a sequence, compose that operation to find all connected sequences, check which tasks stay constant across those sequences, and replace each set of task-equivalent sequences with one quotient coordinate.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="A-local-generator:-swap-two-neighbours">A local generator: swap two neighbours</h2><p>Let <span class="tex">\(\tau_i\)</span> exchange flips at positions <span class="tex">\(i\)</span> and <span class="tex">\(i+1\)</span>. This adjacent swap is a <em>generator</em>: a simple transformation whose compositions produce more complicated transformations.</p></div>

```julia
function swap_adjacent(sequence, i)
    swapped = copy(sequence)
    swapped[i], swapped[i + 1] = swapped[i + 1], swapped[i]
    swapped
end
```

```julia
show_sequence(sequence) = join(ifelse.(sequence, "H", "T"))
```


```julia
    swap_once = show_sequence(swap_adjacent(seed_sequence, 3)),
```

<div class="markdown"><p>Each swap is an <em>involution</em> because applying it twice returns the original sequence: <span class="tex">\(\tau_i^2=e\)</span>, where <span class="tex">\(e\)</span> is the identity transformation. Composition also matters: swapping positions 2 and 3, then positions 3 and 4, can differ from reversing that order.</p><p>For sequences of length <span class="tex">\(n\)</span>, the adjacent swaps generate the <em>symmetric group</em><span class="tex">\(S_n\)</span>, the group of all permutations of <span class="tex">\(n\)</span> positions. Composing two permutations produces another permutation, composition is associative, an identity leaves the sequence unchanged, and every permutation has an inverse. These group properties let us move around a structured family of sequences without changing their values, only their positions.</p></div>

```julia
function permutation_orbit(sequence)
    seen = Set([Tuple(sequence)])
    frontier = [copy(sequence)]

    while !isempty(frontier)
        current = popfirst!(frontier)
        for i in 1:(length(current) - 1)
            candidate = swap_adjacent(current, i)
            key = Tuple(candidate)
            if key ∉ seen
                push!(seen, key)
                push!(frontier, candidate)
            end
        end
    end

    sort([collect(key) for key in seen], by = show_sequence)
end
```

Each swap adds a new sequence only once.</p><p>Change the seed to two heads and two tails. Before running it, how many distinct orderings do you expect? Keep the seed short: enumerating an orbit can grow quickly.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="The-orbit:-every-reachable-observation">The orbit: every reachable observation</h2><p>A group acts on a space when each group element transforms an object in that space. Here, <span class="tex">\(S_4\)</span> acts on four-flip sequences by permuting their positions. The <em>orbit</em> of <code>HHHT</code> is the set of sequences reachable under that action:</p><p class="tex">$$\operatorname{Orb}(x)=\{g\cdot x:g\in S_4\}.$$</p><p>The orbit contains four sequences instead of <span class="tex">\(4!=24\)</span> because exchanging two identical heads does not produce a new sequence. More generally, a sequence with <span class="tex">\(k\)</span> heads has <span class="tex">\(\binom{n}{k}\)</span> distinct orbit members. The orbit reveals which raw distinctions arise only from order.</p><p>We now compare two questions from Chapter 1 across this orbit. <code>is_fair_posterior</code> asks for the probability that the fair coin generated the observed sequence, using the same prior and coin weights as Chapter 1. <code>longest_head_run</code> asks for the largest number of consecutive heads in that sequence. The first query infers a hidden coin type; the second computes a property of the observed data. The table below evaluates both queries for every orbit member so we can check which answers survive a change in flip order.</p></div>

```julia
count_representation(sequence) = (
    flips = length(sequence),
    heads = count(identity, sequence),
)
```

```julia
function is_fair_posterior(sequence)
    likelihood(weight) = prod(flip ? weight : 1 - weight for flip in sequence)
    fair_mass = is_fair_prior * likelihood(fair_weight)
    trick_mass = (1 - is_fair_prior) * likelihood(trick_weight)
    fair_mass / (fair_mass + trick_mass)
end
```

```julia
function longest_head_run(sequence)
    longest = 0
    current = 0
    for s in sequence
        current = s ? current + 1 : 0
        longest = max(longest, current)
    end
    longest
end
```

```julia
orbit_table = [
    (
        sequence = show_sequence(sequence),
        representation = count_representation(sequence),
        fair_posterior = is_fair_posterior(sequence),
        longest_head_run = longest_head_run(sequence),
    )
    for sequence in orbit
]
```

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="Task-invariants">Task invariants</h2><p>A task <span class="tex">\(T\)</span> is <em>invariant</em> under a transformation <span class="tex">\(g\)</span> when</p><p class="tex">$$T(g\cdot x)=T(x).$$</p><p>The fair-coin posterior is constant across the orbit because the conditionally independent coin model assigns the same likelihood to every permutation. The longest-run task varies across the same orbit because it depends on adjacency.</p><p>The transformations tell us which distinctions we <em>could</em> ignore; task invariance tells us which distinctions we may ignore without changing the answer.</p></div>

```julia
function count_decoder(representation)
    n = representation.flips
    k = representation.heads
    fair_likelihood = fair_weight^k * (1 - fair_weight)^(n - k)
    trick_likelihood = trick_weight^k * (1 - trick_weight)^(n - k)
    fair_mass = is_fair_prior * fair_likelihood
    trick_mass = (1 - is_fair_prior) * trick_likelihood
    fair_mass / (fair_mass + trick_mass)
end
```

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="From-an-orbit-to-a-quotient">From an orbit to a quotient</h2><p>Define <span class="tex">\(x\sim y\)</span> when a permutation carries <span class="tex">\(x\)</span> to <span class="tex">\(y\)</span>. This relation is an <em>equivalence relation</em>: every sequence is equivalent to itself, equivalence works in both directions, and equivalences compose. Its equivalence classes are the permutation orbits.</p><p>The <em>quotient space</em><span class="tex">\(X/S_n\)</span> replaces every orbit in the original sequence space <span class="tex">\(X\)</span> with one object. For Boolean sequences of fixed length, the number of heads uniquely labels each quotient class. The map</p><p class="tex">$$q(x)=(\operatorname{length}(x),\operatorname{heads}(x))$$</p><p>is a quotient map. The count representation is therefore a coordinate system for the permutation quotient.</p></div>

```julia
all_boolean_sequences(n) = [
    [isone((mask >> i) & 1) for i in 0:n-1]
    for mask in 0:(2^n - 1)
]
```

```julia
function quotient_classes(states, representation)
    classes = Dict{Any, Vector{Any}}()
    for state in states
        push!(get!(classes, representation(state), Any[]), state)
    end
    classes
end
```

```julia
four_flip_quotient = quotient_classes(
    all_boolean_sequences(4),
    count_representation,
)
```

<div class="markdown"><p>The quotient reduces the 16 ordered four-flip sequences to five coordinates, one for each possible head count. In general, it reduces <span class="tex">\(2^n\)</span> Boolean sequences to <span class="tex">\(n+1\)</span> count coordinates. Their class sizes for four flips are <code>1, 4, 6, 4, 1</code>, the corresponding binomial coefficients.</p><p>If a task is invariant on every class, it <em>factors through</em> the quotient:</p><p class="tex">$$T = D\circ q.$$</p><p>Here, <span class="tex">\(q\)</span> is <code>count_representation</code>, and <span class="tex">\(D\)</span> computes the posterior from a head count. The factorisation makes the task easier because the solver no longer needs separate rules for <code>HHHT</code>, <code>HHTH</code>, <code>HTHH</code>, and <code>THHH</code>. It evaluates one decoder at their shared coordinate <code>(flips = 4, heads = 3)</code>. Across all length-<span class="tex">\(n\)</span> observations, the decoder handles <span class="tex">\(n+1\)</span> inputs instead of <span class="tex">\(2^n\)</span> ordered inputs.</p><p>Try increasing the sequence length from four to five in the quotient cells. Compare the number of raw sequences with the number of head-count coordinates before deciding which space you would want to compute over.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="The-quotient-determines-the-count-distribution">The quotient determines the count distribution</h2><p>The distribution induced on the quotient by the original conditionally i.i.d. sequence model is binomial.</p><p>For a coin with head probability <span class="tex">\(\theta\)</span>, every ordered sequence in the class labelled by <span class="tex">\((n,k)\)</span> has probability</p><p class="tex">$$\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}.$$</p><p>The orbit contains <span class="tex">\(\binom{n}{k}\)</span> such sequences. Summing their equal probabilities gives the probability of the quotient coordinate:</p><p class="tex">$$P(q(X)=(n,k)\mid\theta)
=\binom{n}{k}\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}.$$</p><p>This expression is the probability mass function of <span class="tex">\(\operatorname{Binomial}(n,\theta)\)</span>. Applying the quotient map to the ordered Bernoulli-sequence model therefore produces a binomial count model. We can generate and condition on the quotient coordinate directly instead of constructing an ordered sequence and then counting it.</p></div>

```julia
binomial_head_count(n, weight) = @~ Binomial(n, weight)
```

<div class="markdown"><p>The posterior above conditions <code>is_fair_coin</code> on a count drawn directly from <code>Binomial</code>. Each proposed world chooses a coin type and draws a head count for the observed number of flips. Rejection sampling keeps the coin type when that count matches <code>observed_quotient_coordinate.heads</code>.</p><p>Conditioning on the count gives the same coin posterior as conditioning on the original sequence: the binomial coefficient multiplies both coin likelihoods by the same amount and cancels when we normalise them. That cancellation also explains why <code>count_decoder</code> can omit the coefficient. At the starting settings, the exact probability is about 0.404; the estimate from 300 accepted samples fluctuates around it. Try a seed with two heads, then with four heads, keeping the length fixed. More heads favour the trick coin and lower the fair-coin probability.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="What-the-count-cannot-tell-us">What the count cannot tell us</h2><p>Now ask for the longest uninterrupted run of heads in the observed sequence. The count coordinate records how many heads occurred, but discards where they occurred. The starting orbit makes that loss explicit:</p><table><tbody><tr><th align="left">Sequence</th><th align="left">Count coordinate <code>(flips, heads)</code></th><th align="right">Longest head run</th></tr><tr><td align="left"><code>HHHT</code></td><td align="left"><code>(4, 3)</code></td><td align="right">3</td></tr><tr><td align="left"><code>HHTH</code></td><td align="left"><code>(4, 3)</code></td><td align="right">2</td></tr><tr><td align="left"><code>HTHH</code></td><td align="left"><code>(4, 3)</code></td><td align="right">2</td></tr><tr><td align="left"><code>THHH</code></td><td align="left"><code>(4, 3)</code></td><td align="right">3</td></tr></tbody></table><p>Let <span class="tex">\(L(x)\)</span> denote the longest head run. A decoder that receives only <span class="tex">\(q(x)=(4,3)\)</span> must give the same answer for all four sequences. Hence, it cannot return both <span class="tex">\(L(\mathtt{HHHT})=3\)</span> and <span class="tex">\(L(\mathtt{HHTH})=2\)</span>. No decoder <span class="tex">\(D\)</span> can satisfy <span class="tex">\(L=D\circ q\)</span> for every sequence: the run task is not constant within a permutation orbit.</p><p>The next cells explore what remains uncertain when we know only the count. <code>UniformDraw(orbit)</code> chooses an ordering uniformly from the seed's orbit. Under our conditionally i.i.d. coin model, this uniform draw is the conditional distribution of the sequence given its count: all orderings in the orbit have equal probability under either coin. The first plot samples these orderings; the second applies <code>longest_head_run</code> to each sampled ordering.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><p>For the starting seed <code>HHHT</code>, the first plot should give each ordering roughly one quarter of the samples. The second should split roughly equally between runs of length two and three, because two orbit members give each answer. More samples make those proportions more stable; they cannot reveal which ordering produced the original observation.</p><p>The count and the model thus determine a distribution over possible run lengths, but the count does not determine the observed sequence's run length. Choosing one orbit member, or reporting the mean run length of 2.5, cannot recover that missing answer. If we need both the coin posterior and the exact longest run, we could retain the sequence or compute and store its longest run alongside the count before discarding the order.</p><h2 id="Discussion">Discussion</h2><p>Try <code>HHTT</code> as the seed by setting <code>seed_sequence</code> to <code>[true, true, false, false]</code>. Its orbit has six members. Use <code>orbit_table</code> to predict the proportions of runs of length one and two before sampling. Which task answers remain constant throughout the orbit, and which vary? Why must the binomial count likelihood include all six orderings even though the coin posterior decoder can cancel that factor?</p><p>We chose adjacent swaps because they preserve the coin posterior in this model. For the longest-run task, reversal still preserves the answer: it reverses each run without changing its length. Arbitrary adjacent swaps can split or join runs. Grouping a sequence with its reversal therefore preserves the run task, while grouping all permutations loses too much.</p></div>
